page: Microsoft Azure L128ps_v5 is a storage-optimized virtual machine instance powered by an arm64 processor architecture running under the Microsoft Hyper-V hypervisor. The instance is provisioned with 128 dedicated vCPUs and 1024 GB of system memory, maintaining an allocation ratio of 8 GB of RAM per vCPU. It features substantial integrated local storage, incorporating 23,040 GB of direct-attached NVMe SSD capacity to support high-throughput, low-latency I/O operations without depending solely on remote block volumes.

Hardware capabilities prioritize massive data throughput and parallelism. The instance does not include discrete graphics processing units, centering compute tasks strictly on ARM-based multicore processing. Network provisioning does not bundle complimentary public IPv4 addresses, which requires infrastructure administrators to plan routing or address allocations separately. The 23 TB array of local NVMe SSDs provides dense ephemeral storage directly attached to the host, reducing latency compared to network-attached alternatives.

From an architectural efficiency standpoint, the ARM core design paired with dedicated vCPU execution delivers predictable compute density for scale-out data services. A primary consideration is binary compatibility, as all deployed applications, runtimes, and dependencies must support 64-bit ARM architectures. Given the combined scale of 128 dedicated cores, 1 TB of RAM, and over 23 TB of local NVMe SSD capacity, the L128ps_v5 is suited for high-density transactional databases, distributed NoSQL engines, search indexing clusters, and large data warehousing workloads requiring local low-latency cache and storage.

It operates without discrete GPUs and includes zero complimentary public IPv4 addresses. While workloads must be compiled for ARM64 execution, the combination of 128 dedicated cores, one terabyte of RAM, and direct NVMe storage enables consistent throughput and reduced latency for high-capacity operational databases, distributed caching layers, real-time analytics engines, and large-scale transactional workloads.
